meaning: The god who presides over the Pitṛs (the departed fathers) and rules the spirits of the dead.

phonemes.desc: Palatal y as in “young”; the a is short and open.
The name means “twin” — Yama is the twin of Yamī in the earliest tradition.
In compound names the stem surfaces as yam- — the river Yamunā preserves his twin sister’s name.

pronunciation.note: The lord of the dead was the first mortal — the one who found the path and guards it ever since.

domains.title: God of Death, the First Mortal, Judge of the Dead
domains.subtitle: The King of the Ancestral World
domains.lead: Yama is death’s king in the Indian traditions: the first man to die, who found the way to the fathers’ world and now rules it — and judges who may enter. With his noose and his two four-eyed dogs, he waits at the southern direction, the realm of the ancestors, and his account-book is the oldest audit in human literature.

cards.name: The First Mortal
cards.desc: He died before anyone — the twin who found the path to the fathers and became its king.

cards.name: The Noose
cards.desc: His pāśa, the noose, finds every soul at its hour; none outrun it, though all may beg.

cards.name: The Two Dogs
cards.desc: Śyāma and Śabala, four-eyed, follow his road and report the dead; they guard the way.

cards.name: Judge of the Deeds
cards.desc: In the Mahābhārata and Purāṇas he reads the record of every soul — the karma, weighed without scales.

mythology.lead: Yama’s mythology moves from Vedic pathfinder to epic judge to Purāṇic king of hells. He begins as the twin who chose to die — the first of the race to walk the path — and becomes the stern accountant whose city the dead enter by the southern gate. Buddhism and the epics gave him his tortures and his buffalo; the Veda kept his dignity.

myths.title: The Twin Dialogue
myths.text: The oldest Yama-text is a dialogue: Yama and his twin Yamī, the first two beings, and Yamī’s love for her brother. Yama refuses — ‘the immortals watch’ — and the hymn becomes the charter of exogamy and of the incest-taboo itself, argued between the world’s first twins in the world’s first debate.

myths.title: The Path of the Fathers
myths.text: The funeral hymn sends the dead king along the path Yama blazed, past the two dogs and the waters, to the feast of the fathers where Yama waits with Varuṇa. ‘Leave the sin here, keep the glory’ — the formula of every Vedic funeral, spoken to the first traveller’s successor.

myths.title: The King Under the Earth
myths.text: In the epic’s underworld-book, Yama rules below with his city Saṃyamanī, his account read by Citragupta, his noose and his buffalo — the god of justice who once disguised himself as a crab to test a king. The epic makes him dreaded and fair: the judge who cannot be bribed because he already owns everything.

myths.title: The Lord of the Narakas
myths.text: The Purāṇas enumerate eighty-four hells under Yama’s administration, each a precise torment for a precise sin — the liar’s tongue, the thief’s hands. Yet the same texts insist his justice is karma’s arithmetic, not malice: even the tortures are purification, and release comes in time.

lore.syncretism: The Avestan Yima, king of the golden age who kept death from his realm, is Yama’s Iranian twin — the same name, opposite function: where Yima postponed death, Yama administers it. Buddhism made Yama a dharmapāla, converted in the end by the Buddha’s teaching, and carried him east as Enma in Japan, where he still judges with his mirror and staff.
lore.culturalLegacy: Yama is the ancestor of every Asian judge-of-the-dead: Enma-ō in Japan, Yŏmna in Korea, Yanluo in China — a continuous iconography from the Veda to manga. The word ‘Yamī’ survives in the river Yamunā; and the maxim ‘even Yama’s writ runs by karma’ structures the moral imagination of half the world’s population.
lore.extendedMeditation: Yama: the twin’s name, the first word of mortality. Restored plainly, it reads as what it is — a name without ornament for the fact without ornament. Every other god in this lexicon borrows grandeur; Yama IS, which is why his name is the shortest sentence in Sanskrit.
lore.archaeology: No Yama temples in the Vedic sphere — the ancestor-cult needed no image. But his buffalo and noose carved into the doorposts of death-temples across Nepal and Bali, and the Enma iconography of Japanese temples from Kamakura onward, mark the reach of his cult east.
lore.cult: The śrāddha offerings to the dead are his liturgy — every rice-ball given to the fathers feeds his city’s economy. The great annual rites for the dead across Asia (Obon in Japan, Pitṛpakṣa in India) are his festivals without his name.
lore.iconography: Green or black, riding the buffalo, noose in hand, mace or staff in the other; two four-eyed dogs at his feet; in Tibet and Japan, a mirror that shows the soul its deeds and a register that never errs. His third eye — the eye of the judge — opens in the esoteric forms.
lore.reception: Comparative mythology pairs him with Osiris, Hades, and Mictlantecuhtli as the lord of the dead who began as a mortal; his twin-myth is cited in every study of the incest-taboo’s narrative origins. In modern media he is Asia’s Grim Reaper — feared, respected, and occasionally, in the karmic comedies, outwitted.
